t:
Section 912 of title 10, United States Code (article 112 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), is amended to read as follows:“§ 912. Art. 112. Drunkenness and other incapacitation offenses“(a) Drunk on Duty.—Any person subject to this chapter who is drunk on duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.“(b) Incapacitation for Duty From Drunkenness or Drug Use.—Any person subject to this chapter who, as a result of indulgence in any alcoholic beverage or any drug, is incapacitated for the proper performance of duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.“(c) Drunk Prisoner.—Any person subject to this chapter who is a prisoner and, while in such status, is drunk shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.”
.

fable.w: This section amends the Uniform Code of Military Justice to define punitive offenses for drunkenness and incapacitation, to be punished as a court-martial directs. A tempting reading treats the court-martial as a hearing, but it is a criminal adjudication of service members inside the federal military justice system, not consultation with outside parties before a federal policy decision. There is no comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, outside consultation, or grant of a right to sue.
fable.s: Any person subject to this chapter who is drunk on duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.

qwen_block.w: This section defines criminal offenses under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and establishes penalties for service members. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by non-federal entities in a federal decision-making process. The actors involved are military personnel and military courts, which are part of the federal government.
qwen_block.s: Any person subject to this chapter who is drunk on duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.

opus.w: This section rewrites a Uniform Code of Military Justice article to define drunkenness and incapacitation offenses and leave punishment to a court-martial. Nobody outside the federal government is consulted before a federal decision, and there is no rulemaking, public hearing, advisory panel or grant of a right to sue. Reading the court-martial reference as participation would be wrong: it describes the military's own disciplinary process, not outsiders taking part in a federal decision.
opus.s: Any person subject to this chapter who is drunk on duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.
opus.b: No. A court-martial might look like a formal proceeding involving the accused, but it is part of the military's internal justice system. The section only defines offenses and punishments. Nobody outside the federal government is consulted, and there is no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines criminal offenses and punishments under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. It involves internal military discipline and judicial proceedings for members of the armed forces, who are federal personnel. There is no requirement for consultation or coordination with entities outside the federal government (such as states, the public, or private organizations) before a decision is made. Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: Any person subject to this chapter who is drunk on duty shall be punished as a court-martial may direct.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "court-martial" implies a hearing where the accused participates. However, a court-martial is an internal military judicial proceeding involving federal personnel (members of the armed forces), not a process for outside parties to participate in a federal administrative or policy decision. The definition explicitly excludes intra-governmental processes and focuses on consultation with entities *outside* the federal government (states, public, etc.). Military justice is an internal disciplinary mechanism.
